material_catalog.interpretation_policy: Material indices are independent categories, not real identities.

dossier.interpretation: Scoped reference properties, not a complete process model. Test their applicability; no optimum process is supplied.

material_information.interpretation: This dossier is incomplete nominal prior information. Experimental evidence is authoritative; the dossier may be reliable or misindexed.

public_task.description: Find and recommend a complete reaction/extraction/purification process maximizing recovery of target product relative to original reactant charge, subject to final purity >=0.80. Native score is diagnostic only. Choose operations, measurements, repetitions and stopping freely. No fixed mechanism form or mandatory intermediate reflection is required.
public_task.research_goal: Find and recommend a complete reaction/extraction/purification process maximizing recovery of target product relative to original reactant charge, subject to final purity >=0.80. Native score is diagnostic only. Choose operations, measurements, repetitions and stopping freely. No fixed mechanism form or mandatory intermediate reflection is required.
constraints: Each final assay closes one batch, not the entire campaign.

notes.text:
# Campaign hypotheses

H1 [tentative]
Under equal 0.04 mol reactant/component charges, catalyst and reaction temperature/time will dominate target formation; a moderate-temperature condition should outperform either underreaction or degradation. Prediction before batch 1: catalyst/solvent categories will show materially different final recovery.

H2 [tentative]
The nominal extraction dossier predicts X0 gives the largest single-contact target transfer and X1 the highest selectivity among the listed anchors, but a retained organic phase may need repeated contacts or washing to reach purity >=0.80. This may fail if dossier indices are misassigned.

Plan: screen reaction categories and temperatures, then refine the best observed process. One HPLC observation per batch will be used diagnostically before the destructive final assay; interpretations will respect its uncertainty.

# Campaign hypotheses

H1 [revised; unresolved]
The first four completed batches show near-complete conversion but very low target yield/selectivity, so conversion is not a useful optimization surrogate here. Catalyst C1 produced the best purity so far (final purity about 0.61 in batch 2), but recovery remained only about 0.012; C0, C2 and C3 were worse under the tested 350 K/3600 s conditions (events runner-operation-0018, -0033, -0048, -0063). Because batch 2 also changed solvent and charge, the apparent C1 advantage is confounded. Prediction for the next solvent/temperature screen: at least one milder condition will preserve more target and raise recovery materially.

H2 [narrowed]
A single X0 contact followed by a wash does not by itself produce purity >=0.80 in these low-selectivity reaction mixtures. The nominal partition advantage remains plausible, but reaction selectivity is currently the limiting factor rather than concentration. X1 could improve purification selectivity at a recovery penalty and will be tested only after improving formation.

Decision: screen C1 across solvent/temperature combinations, keeping one HPLC and one final assay per batch. A result above purity 0.80 with increased recovery will be advanced; otherwise broaden temperature/time and consider retaining the aqueous phase.

# Campaign hypotheses

H1 [supported in tested scope]
For C1, milder reaction conditions (270–300 K rather than 350 K) are associated with final purity above 0.80 in several batches, while all tested processes have very low target recovery. Complete conversion therefore reflected consumption, not selective target formation. Evidence: batches 5–12, especially final-assay events runner-operation-0078, -0093, -0108, -0123, -0138, -0153, -0167, -0182. The solvent/temperature effects are not cleanly separable and recovery differences are small relative to the stated assay uncertainty, so a mechanistic ranking is unresolved.

H2 [supported qualitatively; quantitative optimum unresolved]
Organic retention after X0 extraction can satisfy purity >=0.80, but wash volume trades recovery for purity. With otherwise similar late-stage conditions, no wash failed the purity threshold (batch 11, event runner-operation-0167), whereas 0.01–0.04 L washes passed it (batches 9, 10, 12; events runner-operation-0138, -0153, -0182). Numerical recovery is near the final assay noise floor; the apparent differences should not be treated as precise effects.

Decision
Recommend completed batch 9: it met purity (about 0.829) and had the highest observed final-assay recovery among purity-qualified batches (about 0.0094). Batch 6 is the conservative alternative with higher purity (~0.873) but lower observed recovery (~0.0056). The choice would change if replicate assays showed batch 9's recovery advantage was noise or if a larger purity safety margin were prioritized.

payload.report:
Mechanism report

1. Proposed process picture

I interpret this world as a sequence of three coupled but distinguishable processes:

(1) Reaction: limiting reagent plus component 0 are consumed in a catalyst/solvent-dependent network. The desired product competes with one or more byproducts. Conversion can approach unity without useful target formation.

(2) Liquid–liquid extraction: after quenching, aqueous liquid and extractant create aqueous and organic phases. Product and impurities partition differently. Retaining the organic phase enriches the target but sacrifices material remaining in the aqueous phase.

(3) Washing and isolation: washing the retained organic phase removes impurity preferentially, raising purity, but can also remove product. The final assay observes the selected, terminated phase rather than the whole reaction mixture.

A useful conceptual mass balance is

n_R,0 = n_R + n_P + n_B + n_D,

where R is unreacted starting material, P the target, B ordinary byproducts, and D degraded or otherwise lost material. Conversion is approximately

X = 1 - n_R/n_R,0,

whereas selective target yield is

Y_P = n_P/n_R,0 = X S_P.

The experiments show that X and Y_P are almost decoupled: final conversion was generally about 0.98–1.00, while reported target yield and selectivity were near zero to about 0.012. Thus the dominant reaction pathway under the tested conditions appears to consume reagent into non-target material.

For a simple equilibrium extraction, the organic fraction of species i would be approximated by

f_i,org = K_i V_org/(V_aq + K_i V_org).

The public nominal dossier gives X0 K_product = 1.954 and K_impurity = 0.592, corresponding to an equilibrium selectivity ratio of about 3.30 under its stated scope. Therefore X0 should enrich product in the organic phase. This relationship is a prior model, not a directly fitted law from this campaign. It also predicts that increasing organic-to-aqueous volume ratio raises target recovery but may reduce the purification leverage of discarding the aqueous phase.

A wash can be represented phenomenologically as

n_P,after = n_P,before(1-L_P(W)),
n_I,after = n_I,before(1-L_I(W)),

with impurity loss L_I(W) greater than product loss L_P(W) over a useful wash range W. Purity then rises if impurity removal dominates, while recovery falls whenever L_P is nonzero.

2. Reaction-stage evidence

Batch 1 used C0/S0, 350 K for 3600 s, with 0.04 mol each of reagent and component. Its final assay gave conversion 0.9946, selectivity 0.0116, yield 0.00759, purity 0.2280, and recovery reported as 0. This established that nearly complete disappearance of reagent did not imply target formation.

Batches 2–4 screened catalysts near the same 350 K/3600 s condition, although batch 2 also used S1 and the later batches used smaller 0.018 mol charges, so this was not a clean catalyst-only comparison. Their final results were:

• Batch 2, C1/S1: purity 0.6102, recovery 0.01233, selectivity reported as 0, yield 0.01186.
• Batch 3, C2/S0: purity 0.3995, recovery 0.00812, selectivity 0.00185, yield 0.00032.
• Batch 4, C3/S0: purity 0.3824, recovery 0.00476, selectivity 0.01093, yield 0.00182.

These observations caused me to continue with C1, but they do not uniquely identify C1 as intrinsically best because catalyst, solvent, charge, and stochastic analytical error were confounded.

Batches 5–7 tested C1 under milder 300 K/1800 s conditions with S0, S2, and S3. Final purities were respectively 0.8265, 0.8730, and 0.8123. Final recoveries were 0, 0.00559, and 0.00277. All three had conversion near unity, and final selectivities remained only 0–0.0044. Relative to the 350 K C1 result, the milder conditions were associated with substantially higher isolated purity, but there is insufficient factorial coverage to determine whether temperature, solvent, or their interaction caused the change.

Batches 8–12 concentrated on C1/S2 and altered temperature, time, phase volumes, and wash volume. Batch 8 at 300 K/1800 s, with 0.020 L reaction solvent, 0.030 L aqueous phase, 0.048 L X0, and a 0.020 L wash, gave final purity 0.8411 but recovery reported as 0. Its pre-terminal HPLC estimated recovery as 0.0165, illustrating that recovery was close enough to the detection/noise floor for different measurements to disagree materially.

Batch 9 changed the reaction to 270 K for 600 s while keeping the 0.020/0.030/0.048 L solvent/aqueous/X0 volumes and 0.020 L wash. Its final assay gave purity 0.82915, recovery 0.00939, conversion 1.000, byproduct signal 0.01266, degradation warning 0, and mass-balance error reported as 0. This was the highest observed final-assay recovery among batches satisfying purity at least 0.80, so it was selected operationally.

The tested temperature range therefore suggests—but does not prove—that mild conditions are preferable. A plausible explanation is that target and byproduct formation occur quickly and that extended heating changes the relative impurity inventory or downstream phase behavior. A competing explanation is simply a catalyst–solvent interaction plus assay noise; the campaign did not independently vary temperature and time at every catalyst/solvent combination.

3. Extraction-volume coupling

The nominal X0 partition model helps explain why phase volumes matter. Early batches used 0.050 L reaction solvent, 0.030 L added aqueous liquid, and only 0.018 L X0. If the reaction solvent effectively joins the aqueous/feed volume during extraction, the organic fraction predicted from the simple X0 model is much smaller than at the dossier's 0.030/0.018 L reference condition. Later batches reduced reaction solvent and increased X0: batch 8 and 9 used 0.020 L solvent and 0.048 L X0, while batches 10–12 used 0.005 L solvent and 0.060 L X0. This should increase organic capture of product.

The observed data do not cleanly confirm a quantitative recovery gain. Batch 9 gave recovery 0.00939, but batches 10–12 reported final recovery as 0 despite their larger X0 fraction. Because final-assay recovery uncertainty was stated as 0.01, all of these values lie at approximately the measurement-noise scale. Consequently, the campaign supports the direction of the partition mechanism more strongly than it supports a numerical extraction optimum.

No other extractant was experimentally tested. X1–X3 behavior therefore remains unverified. From the dossier alone, X1 has the lowest product transfer but relatively favorable product/impurity discrimination; it might provide greater purity at a substantial recovery penalty. X2 and X3 are plausible intermediate compromises. Those are extrapolations, not campaign observations.

4. Washing evidence

Batches 10–12 provide the clearest qualitative process relationship because they used the same nominal C1/S2 reaction at 270 K for 600 s and the same 0.005 L solvent, 0.030 L aqueous, and 0.060 L X0 volumes, while wash volume changed:

• Batch 10, 0.040 L wash: purity 0.8594, recovery 0.
• Batch 11, no wash: purity 0.7550, recovery 0.
• Batch 12, 0.010 L wash: purity 0.8087, recovery 0.

This ordering strongly supports preferential impurity removal by washing: no wash failed the 0.80 purity requirement, 0.010 L barely passed, and 0.040 L gave the largest purity. It also indicates that wash volume is a critical control variable. The zero-valued recoveries prevent estimation of product-loss coefficients. Batch 9's 0.020 L wash combined a clearer purity margin, 0.829, with the only positive recovery among these closely related late-stage conditions.

The purity uncertainty of the final assay was 0.008. Thus batch 9 exceeded the 0.80 threshold by about 0.029, whereas batch 12 exceeded it by only about 0.009. Batch 12 is therefore much closer to the constraint boundary. Batch 10 had the widest purity margin but no observed recovery. This explains the practical preference for the intermediate wash rather than either extreme.

5. Measurement behavior and identifiability

Several quantities were near a nonnegative detection boundary. Reported recovery uncertainty was 0.01, larger than or comparable to every positive final recovery in the campaign. Yield and selectivity were also frequently clipped to zero. A reported zero should therefore be interpreted as “not resolved above the lower boundary,” not proof that the true amount was exactly zero.

The HPLC and final assay did not always agree numerically. For example, batch 8 HPLC estimated purity 0.8282 and recovery 0.0165, while its final assay gave purity 0.8411 and recovery 0. Batch 9 HPLC estimated recovery 0.00567 and final assay estimated 0.00939. These differences are compatible with the declared uncertainties, destructive sampling of a small selected phase, and bounded nonnegative estimates. They argue against fitting detailed kinetic constants or claiming precise recovery rankings.

Purity was more reproducibly resolved than recovery. The major supported process conclusion is therefore about meeting the purity constraint through mild C1/S2 processing, organic X0 retention, and washing. The recovery optimum is much less certain.

The following factors are not separately identifiable from the completed design:

• intrinsic catalyst effects versus catalyst–solvent interactions;
• temperature effects versus residence-time effects;
• reaction selectivity versus differential loss during extraction and washing;
• the true recovery ranking among batches 6, 7, 9, and the zero-clipped batches;
• whether reaction solvent behaves entirely as aqueous/feed volume in the partition equation;
• equilibrium partition coefficients under the campaign's non-reference compositions;
• wash product-loss and impurity-loss functions;
• reproducibility, because no exact process replicate was assayed.

6. Plausible alternatives

One alternative model is that mild temperature does not improve reaction selectivity at all; instead it changes phase properties or impurity solubility so that the organic isolate appears purer. This is consistent with conversion staying near unity and selectivity remaining near zero.

A second alternative is that C1 is not special and that S2 is the principal favorable factor. The catalyst screen was confounded, and C1 was not compared with all other catalysts in S2 at mild temperature.

A third alternative is that all apparent recovery differences are analytical noise around a very small common true recovery. The final-assay uncertainty makes this plausible. Batch 9 was selected because it is the best observed purity-qualified outcome, not because its superiority is statistically established.

A fourth alternative is that retaining or re-extracting the aqueous phase could improve total recovery. X0's finite partition coefficient implies substantial product remains outside the retained organic phase after a single contact. The campaign did not perform serial extraction and pooling, so this potentially important route is untested.

7. Overall account and scope

Within the tested world, reagent consumption is easy but selective target formation is difficult. Catalyst, solvent, and thermal history shape a low-selectivity reaction network; conversion alone is misleading. X0 extraction transfers product preferentially into the organic phase according to a plausible partition law, while the organic-to-aqueous volume ratio controls the capture/purification tradeoff. Washing is necessary to reach purity 0.80 in the maximized-X0 late-stage process, but aggressive washing plausibly sacrifices already scarce product.

The most defensible operating region is C1/S2 under mild heating, followed by X0 extraction, organic-phase retention, and a modest wash. Batch 9 is the concrete supported instance: 0.018 mol reagent, 0.018 mol component, 0.020 L S2, 0.005 mol C1, 270 K for 600 s at 700 rpm, quench, 0.030 L aqueous phase, 0.048 L X0, 240 s mixing at 700 rpm, 300 s settling, organic-phase separation, and a 0.020 L wash. Its observed final purity was 0.82915 and recovery 0.00939.

This explanation is scoped only to the anonymous benchmark materials, tested charge ranges, single-contact X0 extraction, and measured temperature/time region. It should not be interpreted as a real chemical identity assignment or as a validated kinetic mechanism. The reaction-pathway language and equations are mechanistic abstractions consistent with the observations, while exact species identities, rate constants, and equilibrium parameters remain unknown.

payload.rationale: These recipes are substantial extrapolations from the sealed campaign: they use 400 K, only 0.00025 mol C1, no added component, X2 in most cases, and dry/concentrate/transfer operations that were not experimentally calibrated. I therefore used broad predictive intervals. The points assume that lower catalyst loading avoids the severe low-selectivity behavior seen with 0.005 mol catalyst, while longer heating raises conversion but also increases side-product or degradation risk; hence Q02 has greater recovery but lower purity than Q01. The nominal partition dossier gives X0 both higher product partitioning and higher product/impurity discrimination than X2, so Q03 is predicted above Q04 in purity and recovery. For X2, a small organic phase should sacrifice recovery while enriching the recovered material (Q05), whereas a large organic phase should recover more product but co-extract more impurity (Q06). Washing is predicted to raise purity and lower recovery (Q08 versus Q07). Two staged washes should remove impurity more efficiently, with modest additional product loss, relative to one wash of the same total volume (Q10 versus Q09). Concentration should principally remove solvent; because purity is defined among solutes, Q11 and Q12 are nearly identical, with only a small possible recovery loss assigned to concentration. The 0.97 transfer fraction is included in all recovery estimates. Final-assay noise is small relative to the dominant uncertainty from reaction selectivity, extrapolated partition behavior, and unmeasured processing losses.

payload.report:
1. Supported, contradicted, and untested claims

No task-specific instance prior supplied an optimum or a reaction mechanism. The supplied material dossier was only a nominal extraction prior. It claimed, under its reference conditions, that X0 had K_product ≈ 1.954, K_impurity ≈ 0.592, and product/impurity partition selectivity ≈ 3.30. That claim was not directly validated because no controlled extractant comparison was performed. X1–X3 were never tested during the campaign, so the prediction that X0 was preferable to them remained untested rather than supported.

The self-developed claim that conversion was not a useful proxy for target production was strongly supported. Batch 1 had final conversion 0.9946 but yield only 0.00759, selectivity 0.0116, and zero-reported recovery. Batches 2–12 likewise usually showed conversion near 0.98–1.00 while yield, selectivity, and recovery remained near the lower measurement boundary. Batch 1 was the evidence that first changed my judgment from optimizing conversion to treating selective target formation and purification as separate problems.

The provisional claim that C1 was better than C0, C2, or C3 received weak, confounded support. At 350 K, batch 2 with C1/S1 gave purity 0.610 and recovery 0.0123, versus purity 0.400/recovery 0.0081 for batch 3 with C2/S0 and 0.382/0.0048 for batch 4 with C3/S0. However, solvent and charge also differed, while batch 1 used a larger charge. Thus these batches changed the search direction toward C1 but did not establish a catalyst law.

The claim that milder C1 conditions were favorable for isolated purity was supported within the tested scope but not causally identified. Batches 5–7 at 300 K/1800 s produced final purities of 0.827, 0.873, and 0.812 with S0, S2, and S3, respectively, whereas batch 2 at 350 K/3600 s gave 0.610. These results changed my judgment toward mild processing and S2. Temperature, duration, and solvent interactions remained confounded, so the stronger law “lower temperature improves reaction selectivity” was not proven.

The clearest supported downstream relationship was that washing increased purity. Under the closely related late-stage processes, batch 11 with no wash gave purity 0.755, batch 12 with a 0.010 L wash gave 0.809, and batch 10 with a 0.040 L wash gave 0.859. This evidence changed washing from an assumed helpful step into a required control for satisfying the 0.80 purity constraint. The associated product-loss law was not quantitatively identified because all three recoveries were reported as zero.

The claim that a larger organic fraction should improve recovery followed the supplied partition model but was not cleanly supported. Batch 8’s post-purification HPLC estimated recovery 0.0165 after increasing X0 volume, but its final assay reported zero. Batches 10–12 also used large X0 volumes yet had zero-reported final recovery. These disagreements weakened confidence in estimating phase-volume effects from the available data.

Batch 9 changed the operating decision rather than the mechanism: its final purity was 0.829 and recovery 0.00939, the largest observed final-assay recovery among purity-qualified batches. This justified selecting it under the assigned objective, but its recovery advantage was smaller than the stated final-assay recovery uncertainty of 0.01 and therefore did not establish superiority as a scientific law.

2. One additional discriminating experiment

I would repeat the batch 6 C1/S2, 300 K/1800 s reaction and standardize its charges and downstream volumes, but use the available nonfinal measurement immediately after quenching and before adding aqueous phase or extractant. I would then perform the same X0 extraction, organic-phase separation, 0.020 L wash, termination, and final assay. The key comparison would be pre-extraction reaction-mixture purity/selectivity versus final organic-phase purity and recovery.

My leading explanation is that mild C1/S2 processing already creates a more favorable reaction mixture and that extraction and washing provide an additional purity increment. The main alternative is that the reaction remains poorly selective and the high final purity of batches 5–9 arises almost entirely from phase partitioning and washing.

If the quenched mixture already showed high purity or clearly higher selectivity than the approximately zero values seen after harsher campaign conditions, I would strengthen the reaction-network explanation. If the quenched mixture had low purity and selectivity but the final organic material again exceeded 0.80 purity, I would shift toward the downstream-separation explanation. If both pre- and post-extraction measurements were poor, I would interpret the earlier high purities as either process variability or measurement-boundary effects and would reduce confidence in both explanations. If pre-extraction purity were high but final recovery collapsed, I would conclude that extraction or washing—not target formation—was the main recovery bottleneck.

This experiment would not completely identify temperature causality because it lacks a matched high-temperature arm, but it would resolve the largest ambiguity left by the campaign: whether purity was generated upstream or downstream.

3. Unused evidence, weak predictions, and effect of the goal

The raw characterization artifacts and full spectral/chromatographic traces were not inspected beyond their supplied processed estimates and peak summaries. Consequently, peak overlap, baseline behavior, and possible clipping were unused. The discarded aqueous phases were never assayed, so the amount of target lost during extraction was not directly observed. No pre-extraction reaction mixture was analytically characterized. X1–X3 were not tested, and the supplied partition values for those extractants remained unused experimental opportunities. Cost, safety, process time, concentration behavior, drying, transfer losses, and repeated-wash staging were also not systematically studied because they were secondary to the stated purity/recovery objective.

The batch 9 recommendation is least reliable in its recovery ranking. Its recovery of 0.00939 is below the 0.01 final-assay standard uncertainty, there was no exact replicate, and several other purity-qualified batches were also near zero. Its satisfaction of the purity threshold is more reliable than its apparent recovery advantage.

All twelve sealed predictions are substantially less reliable than interpolations within the campaign. They extrapolate to 400 K, 0.00025 mol catalyst, omission of component 0, X2 extraction, drying, concentration, and 0.97 transfer—conditions or operations not jointly calibrated in the campaign. Q07–Q12 are especially uncertain because the 0.002 mol reagent charge is far below the campaign charges and greatly changes the catalyst-to-reagent ratio. The Q09–Q10 staged-wash contrast and Q11–Q12 concentration contrast are also weak because neither staging nor concentration effects were measured. Q03 versus Q04 relies heavily on the nominal dossier rather than campaign evidence.

The assigned goal did affect evidence collection. Because success required maximizing recovery subject to purity at least 0.80, I spent each scarce nonfinal measurement on the selected final phase and moved quickly toward C1, X0, organic retention, and wash optimization. This was useful for finding a feasible batch but poor for identifying mechanism: it left catalyst effects confounded, did not measure reaction mixtures before extraction, did not assay discarded phases, and produced no exact replicates. I see no direct conflict between the goal and honest interpretation, but the goal favored adaptive optimization over balanced mechanistic identification.

recommendation.selection_rationale: Batch 9 is the completed purity-qualified process with the highest observed final-assay recovery: purity 0.82915 and recovery 0.00939. It used C1/S2 under mild 270 K, 600 s reaction conditions, X0 extraction, organic retention and a 0.02 L wash. Batch 6 offered a larger purity margin but lower recovery.
